extracted.intended_audience: improvisers, actors, comedy performers, and improv teachers
extracted.subtask_description: Practical principles and exercises for improvisational theatre focusing on status, spontaneity, and narrative skills to improve scenes and training. Includes rules of play, specific games, and teaching heuristics.

rubrics_metrics.name: Decide and play with status
rubrics_metrics.description: Before improvising a scene, decide your place in the status hierarchy in relation to other actors; status is an internal confidence/pecking order, not necessarily socio-economic standing.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use status as a lens to analyze interactions and annotate dialogue with status transactions (examples provided). Consider status dynamics in jokes and narratives (when high-status individuals fall, others rise). Try playing explicit status relationships (e.g., master/servant) and variants with proscribed pecking orders. The author recommends deliberately choosing status to shape scenes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Physical markers of status
rubrics_metrics.description: Status usually manifests physically and can be controlled to convey rank or confidence.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Key markers: eye contact (breaking it causes status loss; not making it can cause gain), controlling space (low status shuts own space; high status lets space flow into others), leg position (toes inward = low, toes outward = high), stillness (holding still raises status; fidgeting lowers it). Use these consistently to signal status changes in scenes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use status shifts for comedic and narrative effect
rubrics_metrics.description: Status shifts (high to low, low to high) create social and comic dynamics that can structure scenes and jokes.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Exploit the contrast when a high-status character lowers and others rise (and vice versa). Historical/cultural examples (kings keeping low-status courtiers) illustrate why status contrast can be funny or revealing.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use status-based games to train awareness
rubrics_metrics.description: Practice status through structured games to make status transactions instinctive.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: adding gratuitous swearwords to loosen atmosphere; master-servant games where master can snap and servant dies after 3 snaps; variants with multiple people in a pecking order. These games loosen inhibitions and train players to inhabit status roles.

rubrics_metrics.name: Accept offers: say 'Yes' (and) — never block
rubrics_metrics.description: In improv, always accept ('yes and') offers from scene partners; never block any offers.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Saying 'yes' rewards adventure and progression; saying 'no' rewards safety and stalls scenes. Accepting can be implicit (invent background story) or explicit. The rule is central: yield to offers and build on them instead of negating them.

rubrics_metrics.name: Make interesting offers
rubrics_metrics.description: Offers should be specific and interesting rather than dull or generic.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid bland lines like 'Good morning!'; prefer colorful offers that carry character and situation (example: 'Good morning, great heavens Frank, did they let you out?'). Train to craft offers that give partners rich material to work with.

rubrics_metrics.name: Spontaneity exercises to build speed and imagination
rubrics_metrics.description: Train spontaneous response and idea generation with short, rule-based exercises.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples include: story invention by completing phrases and following rapid questions; association games ('tell me a color', imaginary-box prompts); 'Presents' (pretend to give and react enthusiastically); 'It's Tuesday' (overaccept mundane statements and escalate); 'Yes But' (accept then add a spontaneous 'but' clause). Emphasize quick, unselfconscious answers over trying to be clever.

rubrics_metrics.name: Combat schooling/inhibition to preserve creativity
rubrics_metrics.description: Recognize that formal schooling and social pressures can beat creativity out of people; exercises should counteract this tendency.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Encourage practices where participants are not judged for immature or odd responses. Create environments that reward saying 'yes' and imaginative risk rather than safe, image-protecting answers.

rubrics_metrics.name: Narrative structure: connection and reintegration (Chekhov's Gun)
rubrics_metrics.description: A true story is more than a list of events; it must have re-incorporation or cross-referencing that gives a natural place to stop (Chekhov's Gun principle).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid merely chaining events without linkage. Look for ways to reintroduce earlier elements or create payoff that makes the story feel complete.

rubrics_metrics.name: Exercises to create coherent stories from improvisation
rubrics_metrics.description: Practice generating stories by alternating free association with connection, and by using structured prompts and games that force linkage.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Exercises: collaborative Q&A storytelling with a child; 'random story' where one pretends to have a story and the partner extracts it via yes/no rules; 'connect the story' where one supplies unrelated sentences and the other synthesizes them into a cohesive narrative; list dumps; invent characters in groups; 'automatic reading' (read as if from a found tome); 'experts' interview; 'verbal chase' (unpredictable questioner); 'word-at-a-time' group story-telling; playwright exercise (one directs two others to keep action onstage). Use alternation of free association and connection to produce satisfying narratives.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use persona/automatic techniques to bypass self-censorship
rubrics_metrics.description: Adopt devices (automatic reading, pretending to be a conduit) to reduce performers' sense of ownership and self-censorship over content.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Techniques like imagining you're reading from a tome or 'automatic reading' can make material feel as though it isn't coming from the performer's head, reducing inhibition and increasing willingness to produce odd or risky content.

rubrics_metrics.name: Teaching heuristic: trick students into not caring about content
rubrics_metrics.description: Teachers should persuade students that content isn't important so they will explore freely; the content will take care of itself once processes are followed.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Frame exercises and rules so students focus on process (saying 'yes', making offers, status choices) rather than judging or controlling the material. This reduces blocking and allows imagination to surface.
